2027-07-02.title: Friday of the Thirteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Isaac loved Rebekah, and was comforted after his mother's death
Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good
2027-07-02.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 13 (Year I). First Friday of the month, the day on which many parishes keep Mass, adoration and confession in honour of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. July is the month of the Most Precious Blood in popular devotion. The first reading skips the long story of the search for a bride (Genesis 24:9–61). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-07-02.verse: “Go and learn what this means, ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’ For I have come to call not the righteous but sinners.”
theo: The first reading moves in two steps: from a grave to a wedding. “Sarah lived one hundred twenty-seven years.” She dies at Hebron, and Abraham, the man of faith, does what every human being does: he goes in “to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.” Holy Scripture does not hurry grief. Then he rises and does something practical and dignified: he asks the Hittites for a place to bury his dead. “I am a stranger and an alien residing among you; give me property among you for a burying place.” After more than sixty years in the land God had promised him, the only piece of it Abraham owns is a cave and a field at Machpelah, bought for “four hundred shekels of silver” (Genesis 23:16). It is a lesson in the pilgrim life. The Letter to the Hebrews comments: all these died in faith, and “they confessed that they were strangers and foreigners on the earth,” seeking “a better country, that is, a heavenly one.” Jewish, Christian and Muslim traditions all honour that tomb of the patriarchs. The Church too teaches us to respect the bodies of the dead and to pray at their graves (Catechism 2300). The second part of the reading, from chapter 24, is a very different scene. Abraham is old; he sends his oldest servant to find a wife for Isaac among his own kin, and trusts that God “will send his angel before you.” After the long story of the well and Rebekah's kindness, which the Lectionary leaves out, we see the meeting: “Isaac went out in the evening to walk in the field; and looking up, he saw camels coming.” Rebekah looks up too, sees him, and veils herself. Then comes a sentence of great tenderness: “Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah's tent. He took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.” The covenant goes on through the love of husband and wife. The Church sees in the home built on such love a small image of the love of Christ for his people (Catechism 1602–1605).

The Gospel is the call of a man whom everybody despised. Matthew was a tax collector, one who collected tolls for the Roman authorities and for his own pocket, a collaborator in the eyes of his people. “As Jesus was walking along, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth; and he said to him, ‘Follow me.’ And he got up and followed him.” Mark and Luke tell the same story about a tax collector named Levi, and the Church has long understood that this is the apostle Matthew, the author of the Gospel that we read this week. Two words in the story are worth pausing on: he saw, and he said. Jesus looked at the man behind the counter and saw a disciple. Then comes the dinner, and with it the scandal. Jesus sits at table with “many tax collectors and sinners.” In the East to eat with someone was to accept him as a friend. The Pharisees ask the disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus answers with a proverb and a quotation. The proverb: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” The quotation is from the prophet Hosea: “Go and learn what this means, ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’” Go and learn: the teachers of the Law are sent back to school! God does not want religion without love. And then the mission statement of Jesus: “I have come to call not the righteous but sinners.” On First Fridays the Church thinks especially of the Heart that has this mercy. Since the revelations to St Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial in France in 1673–75, Catholics have honoured the Sacred Heart pierced by the lance, from which came “blood and water,” and many keep the nine First Fridays with Mass and Communion. The prayer of St Paul fits the day: that we may “know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge.”
outline: Ask: where do you meet your grief: do you hurry past it, or do you let God comfort you?
Point 1 · A stranger and an alien
Abraham buries Sarah and owns only a tomb in the land of the promise: we are pilgrims.
Isaac and Rebekah: love in the home is God's comfort in sorrow.
Jesus sees a tax collector and calls him; he eats with sinners, because he came for them.
live: Visit the grave of someone you love this week, or pray for the dead at home, and thank God for their life. Grief offered to God becomes a prayer.
Invite to your table or to a cup of tea someone whom others pass by, a widow, a newcomer, someone who has made mistakes.
2027-07-02.prayer: God of Abraham and Sarah, you comfort those who mourn and you make the love of husband and wife a sign of your faithfulness. Teach us to live as pilgrims, strangers and aliens on earth, looking for the better country that you have prepared. Lord Jesus, who saw a tax collector at his table and said, Follow me, call us from whatever keeps us sitting at our counters. Sacred Heart of Jesus, meek and humble, gentle and merciful, make our hearts like yours, and teach us to desire mercy more than sacrifice. Amen.
altar: On the First Friday many Catholics receive Holy Communion and spend time before the Blessed Sacrament. At every Mass the Lord does what he did at Matthew's table: he sits down with sinners, and gives himself to them. Before Communion we say, Lord, I am not worthy; and he says what he said to the tax collector: Follow me. The Eucharist is the meal of the pilgrim people, bread for the road to the better country, and also a foretaste of the wedding feast of the Lamb, of which Isaac and Rebekah's love is a distant image.

quick: Sarah dies at Hebron; Abraham mourns her, and buys a cave at Machpelah from the Hittites as a tomb.
Abraham sends his servant to find a wife for Isaac among his kin; Isaac meets Rebekah, loves her and is comforted after his mother's death.
Jesus calls Matthew, the tax collector, eats with sinners, and says that he has come to call not the righteous but sinners.
2027-07-02.action: Pray for your dead today, and invite someone who is alone to share a meal.
2027-07-02.question: Do I come to Jesus as one of the sick who need a physician, or as one of the well who need nothing?
kidsaint: Margaret Mary was a French girl who was often ill. When she grew up she became a sister at a convent in Paray-le-Monial. One day, while she was praying in front of the Blessed Sacrament, Jesus showed her his heart, full of love for everyone. He asked her to tell people to love his Sacred Heart and to receive Communion on the First Fridays. Some people did not believe Margaret Mary at first. But her friend, a Jesuit priest called Claude de la Colombière, believed her and helped. Now many people all over the world love the Sacred Heart. Lesson: Jesus loves us with a real heart, and he wants us to love him back.

family.explain: Matthew was a tax collector. Nobody liked tax collectors, because they took people's money. One day Jesus walked by and said to Matthew: follow me. And Matthew stood up and followed! Then Matthew had a big dinner at his house, and Jesus sat down to eat with his friends, even those whom others called sinners. The teachers were cross about this. But Jesus said: I came for those who need me, like a doctor for the sick.
family.intention: We thank Jesus for loving everybody. We pray for those who feel left out, and for all the people in our family who have died.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone at school or in our street who is always left out? How can we sit with them this week?”

illus: In a parish near Thrissur, a retired bank manager had a name for strictness. Customers feared him, and so did some of his own family. After a heart attack he began to come to the First Friday evening Mass, sitting at the back. A year later nobody remembered exactly when it began, but the parish noticed that the school fees of some children were being paid quietly, and the sick were being driven to the hospital. He did not like to be thanked. When the priest asked him what had happened, the old man said: a doctor told me I was ill in my body. The Lord told me I was ill in my heart. I had come to the right clinic. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: God of Abraham, you comfort those who mourn. Lord Jesus, you called Matthew and still eat with sinners. Sacred Heart of Jesus, we trust in you. Amen.
share: I am a stranger and an alien (Genesis 23:4). What helps me remember that this world is not my final home?
He loved her. So Isaac was comforted (Genesis 24:67). Who has comforted me in a time of sorrow, and whom can I comfort?
He got up and followed him (Matthew 9:9). What am I sitting at that I must leave to follow Jesus?
pm.resp: Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.
interc: For those who mourn, and for the souls of the faithful departed.
For husbands and wives, that their love may be a sign of God's faithfulness.
For those who feel despised or excluded, as Matthew was.
For priests who offer Mass and hear confessions on First Fridays.
For our group, that we may desire mercy more than sacrifice.
pm.close: Father, you sent your Son to call sinners. Give us the Heart of Jesus, merciful and humble, that we may follow him all our days. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today's first reading begins with a funeral. Sarah has died, and Abraham goes in to weep for her. The Bible does not tell us to hide our tears. Abraham mourns, and then he does the practical thing. He asks for a place to bury his wife. And we learn something that is almost strange: after all those years with God's promise of the whole land, Abraham owns one cave. I am a stranger and an alien residing among you (Genesis 23:4).

That is the life of faith. We are pilgrims. The Letter to the Hebrews says that the patriarchs confessed that they were strangers and foreigners on the earth, because they desired a better country, that is, a heavenly one (Hebrews 11:13–16). We have homes, jobs and plans, and we should look after them well. But our true home is where Christ is, and our dead are not lost: they have gone ahead of us.

And God comforts his pilgrims through each other. Isaac goes out in the evening to walk in the field. He is grieving for his mother. And he looks up and sees camels coming. Rebekah looks up too. Then the Bible says something simple and beautiful: he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death (Genesis 24:67). Husbands and wives, parents and children, friends: love is the way God consoles. Let us not forget to say to those near us that they are a comfort.

In the Gospel Jesus walks by a tax booth and sees a man. Not a tax collector, not a thief, but a man, and he says: Follow me. Matthew gets up. Then at the dinner Jesus eats with sinners, and when he is criticised he answers: Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick (Matthew 9:12). Go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, not sacrifice. On this First Friday we look at the Heart that was pierced for sinners. If you feel you are too bad to come, this Gospel was written for you. And if you think you are too good to need him, it was written for you too. Let us all come to the physician, and let us make room at our own table for those whom he has called.
kids: Children, a man named Matthew collected taxes, and nobody liked him. One day Jesus walked by and said: follow me. Matthew stood up and went with Jesus! Then he gave a big dinner, and Jesus sat down with all his friends, even those whom others did not like. Some grown-ups were cross. But Jesus said: I came for those who need help, like a doctor for sick people. Jesus loves everybody, and today is First Friday, the day we thank him for his Sacred Heart. Let us be kind to a child who sits alone!

intro: A grave and a wedding, a pilgrim people comforted by love, and the Heart of Jesus that calls the sinner to his table.

sub: One cave in the land of the promise.
A better country, a heavenly one.
q: “I am a stranger and an alien residing among you; give me property among you for a burying place, so that I may bury my dead out of my sight.”
All of these died in faith without having received the promises, but from a distance they saw and greeted them. They confessed that they were strangers and foreigners on the earth,
points.apply: Pray this week for the dead of your family by name, at the grave or at home.

sub: Isaac walks in the field in the evening.
He looked up, and she looked up.
q: Then Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah’s tent. He took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.
So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.
points.apply: Say aloud to someone in your family this week, “You are a comfort to me.”

sub: He saw a man at the tax booth.
Go and learn: mercy, not sacrifice.
q: For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.
As Jesus was walking along, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth; and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he got up and followed him.
points.apply: Spend one hour before the Blessed Sacrament this First Friday, and ask the Heart of Jesus to give you a heart like his.

concl: Abraham buries Sarah as a stranger in the land of the promise, and Isaac is comforted by Rebekah's love: the covenant continues through a home built on love.
Jesus calls Matthew and eats with sinners, because he came not for the righteous but for sinners; the Sacred Heart is the heart of that mercy.
2027-07-02.resolve: Keep this First Friday with Mass, confession or adoration, and share a meal with someone who is alone.
